name: Sliding Window
when: A contiguous range can be updated as its boundaries move.
naive: Enumerate every substring and rebuild its state.
why: Each pointer moves forward at most n times; reuse the previous window.
cost: O(n) time; O(min(n, alphabet)) space
mistake: Shrink with while, not if. For LC 76, use counts: a set loses multiplicity.
diagram: expand right → duplicate? → shrink left → record valid length

name: Two Pointers

problems.title: Two Sum Ii Input Array Is Sorted

when: Sorted order or a boundary rule tells you which end to move.
naive: Try all pairs in O(n²).
why: A comparison eliminates a whole group of impossible pairs.
cost: O(n) time; O(1) extra space for sorted pair sum
mistake: Pair-sum movement requires sorted data. Use long for sums that may overflow.
diagram: left → [2 | 7 | 11 | 15] ← right → compare sum → discard one end

name: Fast / Slow Pointers

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End Of List

when: Two walkers can expose a cycle, midpoint, or fixed gap.
naive: Store every visited node to detect a cycle.
why: In a cycle, the faster walker eventually laps the slower one.
imports: None; ListNode is supplied by the problem
cost: O(n) time; O(1) space
mistake: Compare node references, not values. Guard fast.next before advancing twice.
diagram: slow: +1 node → fast: +2 nodes → meet inside a cycle

name: Binary Search on Sorted Data

problems.title: Find First And Last Position Of Element In Sorted Array
Find Minimum In Rotated Sorted Array

when: An ordered search range can be cut in half.
naive: Scan every value in O(n).
why: After comparing the middle, keep only the half that may contain the target.
cost: O(log n) time; O(1) space
mistake: Do not mix closed and half-open intervals. Rotated arrays require an extra sorted-half check.
diagram: [lo … mid … hi] → compare → keep left or right half

name: Binary Search on Answer

problems.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
Minimize Max Distance To Gas Station
Find The Smallest Divisor Given A Threshold
Minimum Number Of Days To Make M Bouquets

when: Feasibility changes monotonically from false to true as an answer increases.
naive: Try every possible answer and simulate it.
why: Binary search finds the first feasible answer without testing the whole domain.
cost: O(n log M) time; O(1) space for LC 875
mistake: Prove monotonicity. LC 774 uses floating-point bounds and a precision stopping rule.
diagram: infeasible × × × | ✓ ✓ feasible → find first ✓

name: Hashing / Frequency Maps
when: You need membership, occurrence counts, or grouping by a canonical key.
naive: Scan existing keys for each input item.
why: Hashing provides average constant-time lookup and updates.
cost: O(n) expected time; O(k) space for k distinct keys
mistake: getOrDefault reduces branching, not asymptotic work. A set cannot represent counts.
diagram: a a b c → key → count → a:2 / b:1 / c:1

name: Prefix Sum / Running Sum
when: Many range sums share overlapping work.
naive: Sum the entire requested interval on every query.
why: Subtract two cumulative totals to cancel the unwanted prefix.
cost: O(n) preprocessing; O(1) query; O(n) space
mistake: Use the extra leading zero. Subarray counting needs a map of previous prefix frequencies.
diagram: prefix before left ┃ selected range ┃ prefix after right → subtract

name: Difference Array / Range Updates

problems.title: Check If All The Integers In A Range Are Covered

when: Many additive interval updates can be applied before reading final values.
naive: Visit every element for every range update.
why: Record only where an addition starts and ends; prefix-sum once at the end.
cost: O(updates + n) time; O(n) space
mistake: Inclusive [l,r] ends at r+1. Large sparse coordinates need ordered event maps.
diagram: +value at left → constant contribution → −value after right

name: Monotonic Stack
when: Find the nearest larger or smaller value on one side.
naive: Scan to the right independently for each index.
why: Unresolved indices stay in order; each is pushed and popped at most once.
cost: O(n) time; O(n) space
mistake: Store indices when distances matter. Equal values need a deliberate comparison rule.
diagram: unresolved [75,71] → 76 arrives → pop 71 → pop 75

name: Monotonic Queue / Deque

problems.title: Shortest Subarray With Sum At Least K
Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than Or Equal To Limit

when: A moving range needs its best candidate without rescanning.
naive: Scan all k values for every sliding-window maximum.
why: Discard weaker older candidates; evict indices that leave the window.
cost: O(n) time; O(k) space for window maximum
mistake: Use indices to expire candidates. LC 862 uses a deque of prefix sums, not raw values.
diagram: front = maximum → descending candidates → back = newest

name: Heap / Top K

problems.title: Kth Largest Element In An Array
Kth Largest Element In A Stream

when: Repeatedly retrieve an extreme or retain a small best set.
naive: Sort all n values even when only k are needed.
why: A size-k min heap discards values too small to remain among the k largest.
cost: O(n log k) time; O(k) space
mistake: Require 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Heap iteration is not sorted; comparator ties can affect top-word problems.
diagram: insert → size exceeds k? → remove smallest → retain top k

name: Intervals

problems.title: Minimum Number Of Arrows To Burst Balloons

when: Ranges overlap, compete for resources, or must be merged.
naive: Compare every interval with every other interval.
why: Sorting makes overlap decisions local to neighboring ranges.
cost: O(n log n) time; O(n) output space
mistake: Touching endpoints merge for closed intervals; meeting schedules often use half-open intervals.
diagram: sort by start → overlap? → extend previous end → otherwise append

name: Greedy Scheduling / Sorting
when: A local choice can be proved to preserve a globally feasible solution.
naive: Explore every sequence of decisions.
why: Maintain the strongest reachable frontier instead of all possible paths.
cost: O(n) time; O(1) space for Jump Game
mistake: Greedy needs a proof; a locally largest value is not automatically optimal.
diagram: reachable frontier → process reachable index → extend frontier

name: Linked List Manipulation
when: Rewire nodes while preserving access to the unprocessed suffix.
naive: Copy all values into a separate array and rebuild nodes.
why: Save next before redirecting a pointer; dummy heads simplify boundary cases.
imports: None; ListNode is supplied by the problem
cost: O(n) time; O(1) space for full reversal
mistake: Save cur.next before overwriting it. Sublist and k-group variants must reconnect both ends.
diagram: prev ← cur   next → suffix → save next → reverse link → advance

name: Tree DFS
when: A subtree can return a summary to its parent.
naive: Recompute subtree heights separately at every node.
why: Postorder computes each child summary once before combining at the parent.
example: Root with two leaf children → depth 2
imports: None; TreeNode is supplied by the problem
cost: O(n) time; O(h) call-stack space
mistake: Distinguish values returned upward from a global best path. Skewed trees can overflow recursion.
diagram: left summary ↘ parent combines ↙ right summary → return upward

name: Tree BFS / Level Order

problems.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
Find Largest Value In Each Tree Row
Average Of Levels In Binary Tree
Populating Next Right Pointers In Each Node

when: Process nodes in increasing depth or aggregate by level.
naive: Traverse the tree again for every requested depth.
why: A FIFO queue groups nodes by distance from the root.
cost: O(n) time; O(w) queue space, plus output
mistake: Capture queue size before processing a level. ArrayDeque does not accept null.
diagram: root → queue [level 1] → queue [level 2] → queue [level 3]

name: BST Problems

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element In A Bst
Lowest Common Ancestor Of A Binary Search Tree
Search In A Binary Search Tree

when: Left values are smaller and right values are larger under the problem’s BST policy.
naive: Visit every node when searching for a value.
why: The ordering rule eliminates one entire subtree per comparison.
example: BST root 4, left 2, right 7; target 2 → visit 4 then 2
imports: None; TreeNode is supplied by the problem
cost: O(h) time; O(1) extra space for iterative search
mistake: A BST need not be balanced: h can be n. Validation needs ancestor bounds, not just child comparisons.
diagram: target < node → left subtree | target > node → right subtree

name: Backtracking Basics
when: Enumerate combinations by building and undoing a partial choice.
naive: Generate all sequences, then filter invalid ones.
why: The recursion tree encodes choices; undo restores state for the next branch.
cost: O(n·2^n) time including copies; O(n) auxiliary space plus output
mistake: Copy the path when saving it. Duplicate values require sorting and same-depth duplicate skipping.
diagram: choose → recurse → undo → choose next → recurse → undo

name: Backtracking with Constraints

problems.title: Letter Combinations Of A Phone Number

when: A partial solution can be rejected before all choices are made.
naive: Construct every complete arrangement and validate at the end.
why: Prune branches immediately when a constraint is violated.
example: 4 queens → 2 valid boards; a repeated column is rejected immediately
imports: None; boolean arrays cols[n], diag1[2*n-1], diag2[2*n-1]; count starts at 0
cost: Exponential search; O(n) auxiliary state for N-Queens
mistake: Undo every changed constraint. State belongs to the current branch, not all branches globally.
diagram: partial board → conflict? prune × → safe? recurse ↓ → undo

name: Graph BFS / DFS
when: Explore connected components or shortest distances in an unweighted graph.
naive: Repeatedly search the same connected region from every vertex.
why: Mark vertices when discovered so each is processed once.
example: Edges 0–1, 1–2; BFS from 0 visits 0,1,2 at distances 0,1,2
cost: O(V+E) time; O(V) space
mistake: Mark on enqueue, not dequeue. Grid bounds and four versus eight directions depend on the problem.
diagram: start → discover neighbors → mark → enqueue → next frontier

name: Topological Sort / DAG

problems.title: Sort Items By Groups Respecting Dependencies
Find All Possible Recipes From Given Supplies

when: Directed prerequisites constrain the order of processing.
naive: Try every possible ordering and validate dependencies.
why: Remove zero-indegree vertices; their dependents may then become ready.
cost: O(V+E) time; O(V) auxiliary space
mistake: Direction matters: prerequisite → dependent. Fewer than n processed vertices means a cycle.
diagram: indegree 0 → ready queue → remove outgoing edges → unlock dependents

name: Union Find / DSU

problems.title: Number Of Operations To Make Network Connected
Remove Max Number Of Edges To Keep Graph Fully Traversable

when: Connectivity changes as undirected edges are added.
naive: Run a graph traversal after every new edge.
why: Represent each component by a root; compression and size-based union keep trees shallow.
cost: O(α(n)) amortized per operation; O(n) space
mistake: Compare roots before joining. DSU does not directly support edge deletion or directed reachability.
diagram: each node → representative root → union smaller tree under larger root

name: Shortest Path

problems.title: Find The City With The Smallest Number Of Neighbors At A Threshold Distance
Number Of Ways To Arrive At Destination

when: Find a minimum-cost path with nonnegative edge weights.
naive: Enumerate all paths or repeatedly scan every unsettled vertex.
why: Dijkstra expands the cheapest known unsettled state using a priority queue.
example: 0→1 costs 2, 0→2 costs 5, 1→2 costs 1 → distance to 2 is 3
cost: O((V+E) log V) time for a simple graph; O(V+E) space
mistake: Negative edges break Dijkstra. LC 787 must track stops; ordinary node-only Dijkstra is insufficient.
diagram: source 0 → cheapest frontier 2 → relax edge +1 → destination 3

name: MST / Graph Greedy

problems.title: Min Cost To Connect All Points
Optimize Water Distribution In A Village
Find Critical And Pseudo Critical Edges In Minimum Spanning Tree

when: Connect all vertices as cheaply as possible, or grow connectivity in weight order.
naive: Enumerate spanning trees and compare total costs.
why: Kruskal takes the cheapest edge that joins two different components.
example: Triangle weights 1,2,5 → choose 1 and 2 → MST cost 3
imports: java.util.Arrays, java.util.Comparator; DSU find/union from pattern 22
cost: O(E log E) time; O(V) DSU space, plus sorting
mistake: MST is not a shortest-path tree. LC 778 and 1102 are bottleneck connectivity variants.
diagram: sort edges by cost → join different components → stop after V−1 joins

name: Trie

problems.title: Design Add And Search Words Data Structure

when: Many words share prefixes and queries follow characters from the start.
naive: Scan every word for each prefix query.
why: A prefix tree shares common character paths.
example: Insert cat and car → shared c→a, then branch t / r
cost: O(L) insertion/query; O(total inserted characters × alphabet) worst-case storage
mistake: This array implementation assumes lowercase a–z. A prefix node is not necessarily a complete word.
diagram: root → c → a ↗ t(end) / ↘ r(end)

name: Bit Manipulation
when: Information can be encoded or canceled bit by bit.
naive: Use a frequency map to find the value occurring once.
why: XOR cancels pairs because x XOR x = 0 and x XOR 0 = x.
code:
int answer = 0;
for (int x : nums) answer ^= x;
cost: O(n) time; O(1) space for paired duplicates
mistake: This XOR trick requires all other values to appear twice. LC 137 needs per-bit counts or a state machine.

name: 1D DP Basics
when: A one-dimensional state summarizes smaller overlapping subproblems.
naive: Recursively recompute the same prefix solutions.
why: Store each state once, then build larger answers from known states.
cost: O(n) time; O(1) space for House Robber
mistake: Define the state before coding. Rolling variables must be updated in the correct order.
diagram: best[i] = max(skip → best[i−1], take → best[i−2]+value)

name: Knapsack / Subset DP
when: Choose items subject to capacity, target sum, or multiple resource limits.
naive: Enumerate all subsets of items.
why: Merge equivalent partial subsets into a state indexed by capacity.
example: [1,5,11,5], target half=11 → reachable → equal partition exists
cost: O(n·target) time; O(target) space for 0/1 subset sum
mistake: Iterate capacity downward for one use per item. Unbounded coin combinations use ascending capacity.
diagram: item → [reachable sums] → update backward → avoid reusing item

name: Grid DP
when: A cell depends on already solved neighboring cells in an acyclic direction.
naive: Enumerate every path through the grid.
why: Combine predecessor answers once per cell.
example: 3 rows × 7 columns, right/down moves → 28 unique paths
imports: java.util.Arrays; rows and cols must be positive
cost: O(rows·cols) time; O(cols) space
mistake: Initialize boundaries deliberately. Obstacles need dp[col]=0; path counts may require wider integers.
diagram: from above ↓ + from left → current cell → continue row by row

name: String DP / Sequence DP

problems.title: Minimum Insertion Steps To Make A String Palindrome

when: Two prefixes or an interval describe repeated sequence subproblems.
naive: Enumerate all subsequences and compare them.
why: A pair of prefix lengths is enough to reuse previously solved comparisons.
example: abcde and ace → LCS ace → length 3
cost: O(mn) time; O(mn) space for LCS
mistake: Subsequence allows gaps; substring does not. Empty prefixes belong in the base row and column.
diagram: matching chars → diagonal +1 | mismatch → max(up, left)
